destination.title: A billionaire heard his own voice on an FBI tape

short24: To catch a billionaire trader, the FBI used the same tool it used on the mob: wiretaps.
Raj Rajaratnam ran Galleon, a hedge fund that peaked near seven billion dollars.
His sources sat inside the companies — an Intel executive, a McKinsey partner, an IBM executive — each charged separately.
It was the first big insider case built on court-authorized wiretaps.
Prosecutors played the jury his own phone calls — the scheme in his own voice.
On May 11, 2011, a jury convicted him on all fourteen counts.
He got eleven years — at the time, prosecutors called it the longest insider-trading sentence in U.S.
history — and had to forfeit nearly fifty-four million dollars.
In 2013 an appeals court upheld the wiretaps as lawful.
A separate trial even convicted a Goldman Sachs director of feeding him secrets.
Watch the full story on the channel.

candidate_payload_lines: Conviction/sentence stated as fact; underlying conduct framed as "the jury found / prosecutors proved / the government said".
DO NOT conflate co-defendants — Gupta is a separate case (CLM-0011).

He ran the fund like a newsroom that never went to sleep, pulling in fragments from everywhere, rewarding whoever brought him something sharp, and never quite forgetting whoever showed up empty-handed.
None of them, on a normal Tuesday, looked anything like a criminal.
If the story had simply stayed there, in that comfortable shadow, you would never have heard this man's name.
This matters to you even if you have never bought a single share in your life.
That nobody at the table can simply see the cards.
Tired of watching the pattern light up, again and again, and never being able to reach the people behind it.
And to do it, they reached for a tool that, until that moment, no one in the country had ever really aimed at a man in a good suit.
The quiet genius of a network like this is that nobody inside it ever has to feel like a criminal.
It is the chance to take the one thing the market is never, ever supposed to sell, a sure thing, and to feel, just for a moment, like a person who simply cannot lose.
And in 2008, on Raj Rajaratnam's phone, the recorders began to turn.
Patience, it turned out, was the one weapon the men at the top had never planned for.
People discussed information they were never supposed to have.
The question waiting at the end of this case was never only whether one man had done it.
On the morning of October sixteenth, 2009, it ended the way these things end in the movies, except that it was completely real.
Because the one thing that had truly held it all together had never been the trades.
He hired one of the finest defense teams that money can buy, and then he made a choice that most people in his position never make.
era_note: SET THIS. Modern stock footage is only usable if the case is modern; a 1960s case dressed in present-day footage reads wrong.

shorts.angle: The argument that had protected the top of Wall Street for a generation died the moment the tapes were played.
shorts.type: C - the defense, and the recording that ended it
shorts.avoids: short24 states that the wiretaps existed and that the jury convicted on all fourteen counts. It never names the defense those tapes destroyed, or why it had worked for so long.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: A wiretap on a man in a good suit. How did a federal judge ever agree to that?
shorts.loop_join: L5 lands on the word mosaic and L1 opens by naming the mosaic theory, so the last phrase and the first sentence close on each other.

lines.text: The defense had a name for its argument. The mosaic theory.
source_lines: The defense even had a name for its argument. The mosaic theory.

lines.text: The idea that a brilliant analyst builds a picture out of a thousand small, public, perfectly legal pieces, the way a mosaic is built from tiles.
source_lines: The idea that a brilliant analyst builds a picture out of a thousand small, public, perfectly legal pieces, the way a mosaic is built from tiles

lines.text: For years that picture had been almost impossible to take apart. It was the perfect defense for an invisible crime.
source_lines: For years, that picture had been almost impossible to take apart. It was the perfect defense for an invisible crime.

lines.text: The trouble, this time, was simple. The tapes did not show a mosaic. They showed a phone call. The jury did not have to imagine the crime. They could hear it.
source_lines: The trouble, this time, was simple. The tapes did not show a mosaic. They showed a phone call.
The jury did not have to imagine the crime. They could hear it.

lines.text: The deniable phone call had become a recording. Time-stamped, in the speaker's own unmistakable voice, sitting in a government evidence locker.
source_lines: Now it was on tape. The whisper had a waveform.
The deniable phone call had become a recording — time-stamped, in the speaker's own unmistakable voice, sitting in a government evidence locker, waiting.

lines.text: The trial opened in Manhattan in 2011, and more than anything else, it turned on sound.
source_lines: The trial opened in Manhattan in 2011, and more than anything else, it turned on sound.

lines.text: Prosecutors did not describe the scheme in their own words. They sat twelve ordinary people down and played the recorded calls, again and again.
source_lines: The prosecutors did not simply stand up and describe the scheme in their own words. They played it.
They sat the jury down, and they let twelve ordinary people listen to the defendant's own recorded phone calls. Again, and again.

lines.text: You cannot tell a jury a recording is only guessing, or jealous, or assembling a clever mosaic of public facts.
source_lines: You cannot say the tape was confused, or jealous, or just assembling a clever mosaic of public facts.

shorts.angle: You do not have to own a single share for this one to have been taken out of your pocket.
shorts.type: A - the detail that makes it about the viewer
shorts.avoids: short24 is the case summary: the fund, the sources, the wiretaps, the sentence. It never explains who was on the other side of those trades, or why a pension holder was in the game without knowing it.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: You can see the suspicious trade on a chart. How do you ever prove a whisper?
shorts.loop_join: L5 asks who actually pays, and L1 answers on the restart: you do, through the pension and the retirement account you never thought about.

lines.text: This matters to you even if you have never bought a single share. Your pension owns stocks. Your retirement account owns stocks.
source_lines: This matters to you even if you have never bought a single share in your life.
Your pension owns stocks. Your retirement account owns stocks.

lines.text: The savings of almost everyone you know ride on one promise. That the market is roughly fair. That nobody at the table can see the cards.
source_lines: The savings of almost everyone you know are quietly riding on one promise.
That the market is roughly fair. That nobody at the table can simply see the cards.

lines.text: On the other side of his trades sits someone ordinary. A retired teacher. A nurse moving her savings into the market. They think the game is fair.
source_lines: On the other side of his trades sits someone completely ordinary.
A retired teacher. A nurse moving her savings into the market.
They are playing what they think is a fair game, and they have no idea that the game is not fair.

lines.text: Not a vault broken open in the night, but a market tilted in broad daylight, one secret at a time, against everyone who actually followed the rules.
source_lines: Not a vault broken open in the night, but a market tilted in broad daylight, one secret at a time, against every single person who actually followed the rules.

lines.text: An insider learns a company is about to be bought. He picks up the phone.
source_lines: An insider learns that a company is about to be bought. He picks up the phone.

lines.text: Days later the deal is announced, the price jumps, and the whisper is worth millions.
source_lines: Days later, the deal is announced to the public. The price jumps. The position that was bought on a whisper is suddenly worth millions more than it cost.

lines.text: The market becomes a private club with a public entrance, and the rest of us pay full price.
source_lines: When a handful of insiders can see them, the market stops being a market. It becomes a private club with a public entrance, and the rest of us are standing in that entrance, paying full price for a seat in a game that was already decided.

lines.text: Regulators could see the suspicious trade. Proving a specific person knew a specific secret is a different thing. So who actually pays for a market that is not fair?
source_lines: Regulators could see the suspicious trade.
But seeing a pattern is not the same as proving that a specific human being knew a specific secret.
